title: Sixty Five Days Without Food
quote: They haven't eaten anything except a little snow since they arrived at the colony nearly 2 months ago. ... The males rely entirely on the body fat that they laid down during summer to survive the long winter fast. ... It takes 65 to 75 days for the eggs to hatch ... by the time the chicks appear, their fathers have fasted for 4 months! ... the egg is kept toasty warm at about 38 °C while the outside temperatures can drop well below -35 °C. ... When the females finally return to the colony in July the males have lost nearly half their body mass.
correctedFact: A male emperor penguin spends the Antarctic winter with an egg balanced on his feet while temperatures drop well below minus 35 Celsius. The egg takes 65 to 75 days to hatch, and by then he has gone about four months without a meal, living on summer fat and losing nearly half his body mass.
note: 65 days is the incubation alone; the fast starts about 2 months earlier and totals about 4 months. Page gives below -35 C, not -40, and no wind speed; huddle rotation cut as a second point.

title: A Species That Fits in a Town
pageTitle: Pictures: Activist's Art Puts Spotlight on Tiger Threats
quote: A century ago 100,000 tigers roamed across Asia from Turkey to the Russian Far East, and south to the islands of Indonesia, across the borders of 30 nations. Since then the big cats have vanished from almost 95 percent of their former range, and just 3,000 or so survive in fragmented pockets of tiger territory scattered across 13 countries.
correctedFact: Around 5,500 tigers are left in the wild, and that is the entire species. A century ago an estimated 100,000 roamed Asia, from Turkey to the Russian Far East and south to the islands of Indonesia. Since then tigers have vanished from almost 95 percent of their former range.
note: The 5,574 figure is from another page, WWF Tigers Alive Annual Report 2023 (https://wwftigers.shorthandstories.com/tigers-alive-annual-report-2023/): 'the Global Tiger Forum that there are estimated to be 5,574 tigers in the wild'. Nat Geo's 13 countries is tied to its older ~3,000 count, so 'thirteen countries' dropped; extinct subspecies cut as a second point.

title: Striped to the Skin
publisher: The Conversation (Andrew Cushing, Assistant Professor in Zoological Medicine, University of Tennessee)
quote: When we have to sedate a tiger to treat an injury or do dental work, we shave their fur. It's always surprising to see that their skin almost looks like it's been tattooed: It has the same striped pattern as its fur! ... Every tiger has its own unique stripe pattern ... This allows researchers who study them in the wild to identify and count individual tigers. They use remote cameras to take pictures of the animals when they walk by. Using this method, tiger experts estimate that only about 3,400 wild tigers remain across their Asian homeland.
note: A zoo veterinarian's first-hand account supports the shaved-tiger hook and the camera-trap counting. Bonus on the page: the stripes are not the same on both sides.

title: It Can Live Without Drinking
publisher: LafeberVet (Anna McRee, DVM; reviewed by Sandra Mitchell, DVM)
quote: Free-ranging fennecs can go without water indefinitely, however fruit, leaves, and roots serve as the sole source of moisture. ... Although fennec foxes will drink freely when given the opportunity, laboratory studies suggest that free-ranging fennecs can survive indefinitely without access to free water. ... Fennecs only lose heat through panting when environmental temperature exceeds 35°C (95°F). ... Fennec foxes are nocturnal hunters that dig burrows as shelter to sleep during the day.
correctedFact: A wild fennec can get by indefinitely without drinking free water. Fruit, leaves and roots supply its moisture, and it sleeps through the hot day in a burrow. It even holds off panting until the air passes 35 Celsius. Offer one water, though, and it will happily drink.
note: Hook supported, but the card's urine-concentrating kidneys, cool humid den air and 'nothing to drink in most of its range' are not on the page. Vet-written sheet; fetched at ?p=39792, which resolves to this sheet.

title: Captive Ones Are Harmless
pageTitle: Toronto Zoo | Blue poison dart frog
quote: In captivity, they primarily eat crickets and fruit flies. The toxic compounds in the skin of D. azureus, known as lipophilic alkaloids, come from their prey, especially ants. ... In captivity, this species loses its poisonous properties because its diet lacks these toxic compounds. ... The skin is covered with a myriad of glands that secrete alkaloid poisons.
correctedFact: A blue poison dart frog does not make its own poison. The alkaloids in its skin glands come from its wild prey, especially ants. In captivity it lives mostly on crickets and fruit flies, and without those toxic meals it loses its poisonous properties.
careAdvice: which is why keeping one is possible at all and why a wild-caught animal is a completely different proposition
note: Page names crickets and fruit flies, not springtails, and says 'loses its poisonous properties' rather than 'effectively non-toxic'; mites as a source come from the PNAS paper, not this page.

title: It Takes Food From Animals Twice Its Size
publisher: National Park Service, Sequoia National Park Nature Guide Service (Walter Fry, Bulletin No. 15, 1923)
pageTitle: Sequoia Nature Guide Service Bulletin No. 15: The Wolverine
quote: July 30, 1906 - Two adult bear, one black and one brown, gave over to one adult wolverine, with excitement and great haste at Buck Canyon, the carcass of a cow upon which they were feeding. ... September 30, 1908 - One large and one medium-sized mountain lions were feasting on a deer that they had recently killed at Willow Meadows, but after much growling and threatened resistance on the part of the larger lion both gave way to the approach of one medium-sized wolverine. ... That the wolverine ranks as king beast of the Sierras, to me there is not a shadow of doubt.
correctedFact: In 1906 Sequoia National Park's nature guide hid and watched a single wolverine take a cow carcass from two bears, which gave it up in great haste. His records add a pair of mountain lions abandoning their fresh deer kill when one wolverine approached. He named it king beast of the Sierras.
note: Eyewitness accounts (1906 to 1908) in a 1923 NPS bulletin; OCR typos fixed in quote. Wolves dropped: the USFS chapter from the first pass says wolves sometimes kill wolverines.

title: Grip Like a Lion's Bite
pageTitle: Coconut crab pinches like a lion, eats like a dumpster diver
quote: A big coconut crab snaps its outsized left claw as hard as a lion can bite, new measurements suggest. ... The strongest claw grip the researchers measured squeezed with a force of about 1,765 newtons ... For comparison, a lion's canines bite with 1,315 newtons and some of its molars can crunch with 2,024 newtons, a 2007 study calculated. ... Birgus latro, the largest known crab species on land
correctedFact: The coconut crab is the largest known crab on land, and its outsized left claw pinches about as hard as a lion bites. The strongest grip researchers measured hit about 1,765 newtons, more than a lion's canine bite of 1,315 newtons and not far short of its molars at 2,024.
note: Card's 'over 3,000 newtons' was the PLOS ONE estimate for a 4 kg crab, not a measurement. Page also says cracking a coconut 'takes hours', against the card's 'easily'. Fetched via sciencenews.org/?p=21648, which redirects here.

title: Japan's Living Snowball
publisher: BirdLife International (text and photos by HIH Princess Takamado, from Fujingahou Magazine)
quote: The subspecies of Long-tailed Tit found in Hokkaido Japan, known as Shima-Enaga in Japanese, is becoming increasingly popular lately. ... Shima-Enaga has a white face and a round, fluffy, snowman-like shape when facing forward. It therefore seems miraculous that Long-tailed Tits, which weigh only 8 grams, live in Hokkaido, where winters are harsh, and its shining appearance makes it look like a real-life 'snow fairy'.
correctedFact: The shima enaga is a real wild bird, the Hokkaido subspecies of long-tailed tit, nicknamed a real-life snow fairy. It has a white face, and when it faces you its round, fluffy body looks like a tiny snowman. Its pale head has long inspired nature lovers.
note: Source says snowman-like, not snowball, and does not tie the fluffiness to winter insulation; juvenile eye markings are only on the Canon page from the first pass.

title: From Venom to Ozempic
publisher: British Journal of Dermatology (Dyson, Lee and Levell, 2026 abstract HX05)
pageTitle: HX05 From toxic bite to therapeutic benefit: the Gila monster and the history of glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists
quote: Interest arose from its extreme metabolic efficiency, with it consuming only three to four meals annually. ... In 1992, endocrinologist Dr John Eng isolated exendin-4 from salivary glands. ... Eng partnered with Amylin to develop exenatide (Byetta), which became the first FDA-approved GLP-1 agonist for type 2 diabetes mellitus in 2005. Longer-acting agents followed, including semaglutide (2021). ... The Gila monster ... underpinned therapeutics that have transformed obesity management.
correctedFact: A Gila monster can get by on just three or four meals a year, and that thrift made scientists curious. In 1992 John Eng isolated exendin-4 from its salivary glands. It became exenatide, the first FDA-approved GLP-1 drug for type 2 diabetes, and longer-acting drugs such as semaglutide followed.
note: Abstract read via CiteDrive mirror. It names semaglutide, not the brand Ozempic; the title stands only on semaglutide being Ozempic's drug, which is not on this page. Tail fat storage unsupported, cut.
